simplifies.crew: This game has 3 crew members. A real base would have many more people and jobs.
simplifies.sols: Our short sols are game rounds. Real storm clouds take several days to reach Mars; we squeeze that into a sol or two.
simplifies.costs: Job costs (power, food, the size of each bar) are game numbers we chose so the game is fair and fun.
simplifies.dose: The space-ray meter uses game units. Which storm is huge and which is small comes from real readings.
simplifies.forecast: Earth's storm warning is a computer forecast, not a measurement. Our dust forecast is made up for the game.
simplifies.dates: Normal Mars radiation was measured in 2012–13; the big storm happened in 2024.
simplifies.real: Real: three dated solar storms measured on Mars, the dust effect on solar panels, the radio delay, and the landing places.
simplifies.storms: Each storm is compared only with the quiet level just before it, on the same detector. A small storm is played as 3 times a normal day for a whole sol; its real peak lasted hours.
simplifies.sites: Site numbers (sun, dust, heater, ice) and upgrade numbers are game numbers. The real record of each place decides which way they lean.
simplifies.moon: On the Moon, the day the Sun hides behind a ridge and the days Earth is hidden are game events. So is the power cut of the 2018 dust storm.
simplifies.risk: In the game, Earth's burst forecast is always right, because we replay history. Real forecasts give a chance and can be wrong.
simplifies.rover: The rover map uses the real colours of a NASA picture, but one square is about 20 km. A real rover drives far less; rocks, rough ground and sample spots are game rules.

sol.title: Sol
sol.text: A sol is one day on Mars. It is about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day.

power.title: Power
power.text: Solar panels turn sunlight into power. Jobs inside the base use some.

air.title: Air
air.text: The air machine makes air to breathe. It needs power every night.

dose.title: Space-ray meter
dose.text: Space rays come from the Sun and from deep space. Scientists call them radiation. Too much is bad for astronauts, so keep this meter low.

food.title: Food
food.text: The greenhouse grows food under lamps. With no food, an astronaut gets too tired to work.

dust.title: Dust
dust.text: Mars dust settles on solar panels. Dusty panels make less power. A dust storm cut a real lander's power by about a third.

burst.title: Space-ray storm
burst.text: Sometimes the Sun blasts out space rays. They reach Mars in under an hour. That is too fast for Earth to warn you.

stormCloud.title: Storm cloud
stormCloud.text: A storm cloud is a huge gas cloud from the Sun. It takes days to reach Mars. So Earth can see it coming and warn you.

askEarth.title: Ask Earth
askEarth.text: Your message takes about 12 minutes to reach Earth. Scientists study it overnight. Their answer is waiting for you in the morning.

teacher.title: For teachers
teacher.goal: On Mars, every choice costs something, and help from Earth can't always arrive in time.
teacher.howTo: Play one mission (about 8 minutes). Talk about the questions. Then play again.
teacher.q1: Who waited for Earth's answer? Was it worth the wait?
teacher.q2: Which skipped job hurt your base the most? How did you find out?
teacher.q3: Why can Earth warn you about a storm cloud but not about a space-ray storm?
teacher.real: The 20 May 2024 solar storm measured by Curiosity, normal Mars radiation, dust storms cutting solar power, and the Earth–Mars message delay are real NASA science. Job costs and storm lengths are game numbers.

commander.intro: Welcome to Ares Station, cadet! I'm Commander Nova. I'm so glad you're here.
commander.intro_moon: Welcome to Artemis Outpost, cadet! I'm Commander Nova. I'm so glad you're here.
commander.who: I lead this crew. Every sol, I pick who does which job. A sol is one day on Mars. It is about 40 minutes longer than a day on Earth.
commander.lore_moon: In 1969, Apollo 11 landed the first people on the Moon. 12 astronauts have walked here.
commander.lore2_moon: NASA's Artemis missions plan to bring people back, near the south pole. Just like us!
commander.who_moon: I lead this crew. Every day, I pick who does which job. One day and night on the Moon lasts about a month! So we count Earth days.
commander.drillIntro: Let's practise calling Earth! Earth moves across the sky. Turn the dish with A and D, or the arrow keys. When it points at Earth, send!
commander.win: Message sent! On the mission, the Ask Earth job works like this. In our game, Earth's answer comes the next morning.
commander.drillIntro_moon: Let's practise calling Earth! Send a message. Watch it fly to Earth and back!

mission.storm: Our mission lasts 5 sols. Keep all 3 astronauts safe, and collect science for the science star. We replay a real storm from the Sun. Nobody knows which sol!
mission.dust: This mission lasts 6 sols. First, you choose where to land. All three places are real. One is known for cold nights. One is known for dust on the panels. One has wind that can blow the panels clean.
mission.moon: Welcome to the Moon's south pole! We stay 5 days. First, choose a landing spot. Sun, ice, a view of Earth: no spot has all three.

engineer.intro: Hey, cadet! I'm Kai, the engineer. If it hums, I probably fixed it.
engineer.who: I grew up fixing bikes. Now I fix a whole Mars base! Mars dust is my enemy. It covers our solar panels.
engineer.intro_moon: Hey, cadet! I'm Kai. Careful, you weigh much less up here. Don't bounce into my tools!
engineer.lore_moon: On the Moon, you weigh about six times less than on Earth. You could jump really high!
engineer.lore2_moon: Apollo astronauts said Moon dust smelled like spent gunpowder. It got into their spacesuits.
engineer.who_moon: I grew up fixing bikes. Now I fix a whole Moon base! Moon dust is my enemy. It is sharp and sticky, and it covers our solar panels.
engineer.drillIntro: Let's practise! The wind keeps blowing dust back onto the panels. Get every panel clean at the same time!
engineer.win: Spotless! On the mission, use the Clean solar panels job. It gives full power the next day.
engineer.drillIntro_moon: Let's practise! At the south pole, the Sun stays low. Turn the panel to face it!
engineer.win_moon: The panel faces the Sun! On the mission, use the Clean solar panels job. It gives full power the next day.

mission.storm: Power is like our pocket money. Sunlight fills it up, and every machine spends it. In our game, the air machine needs power every night. Without it, the air runs low.
mission.dust: Dust is our big enemy here. It falls on the panels every sol, so they make less power. In our game, a dust storm lasts 2 sols. Then the panels make much less power. Real storms last much longer! Save some power before it hits.
mission.moon: Here the Sun stays low in the sky. Crater walls throw long shadows. On a shadow day, our panels make almost no power. Keep some power saved.

scientist.intro: Hello! I'm Amara. I study Mars rocks, and I grow our food.
scientist.intro_moon: Hello! I'm Amara. I study Moon rocks, and I grow our food.
scientist.who: Long, long ago, Gale Crater held a lake. Its rocks still have layers from that water. I read them like a book.
scientist.lore_moon: Some craters near the south pole never see the Sun. They are among the coldest places we know.
scientist.lore2_moon: Their ice may be billions of years old. Ice means water, air and even rocket fuel!
scientist.win_moon: A harvest! Plants need water and light. Here, that light comes from our power.
scientist.who_moon: Moon rocks are very, very old. Crashing space rocks dug the craters and threw rocks all around. I read them like a book.
scientist.drillIntro: Let's practise! Thirsty plants stop growing. Water each plant before it dries out.
scientist.win: What a harvest! On the mission, the greenhouse needs power for its lights. Then it grows food.
scientist.drillIntro_moon: Let's practise! Press the ice to melt it. The cold freezes it back!

mission.storm: Science trips outside earn science. But outside, you get more space rays. The greenhouse grows food, if its lights get power.
mission.dust: Cold nights need the heater, and the heater needs power. In our game, if the heater stops, our plants freeze! On the last sol, the rover can drive out for rock samples. The far crater gives more science, but costs more power.
mission.moon: Some craters here never see the Sun. Scientists think they hide ice. Ice can give us water and air. Landing near ice is cold and dark, though.

drone.intro: Beep boop! I'm Pip, the station drone. I watch the Sun for you.
drone.who: I was built to read space weather. Sometimes the Sun throws out tiny, very fast bits. We call them space rays.
drone.intro_moon: Beep boop! I'm Pip. I watch the Sun. I keep an eye on Earth up there, too.
drone.who_moon: The Moon has no thick air to stop space rays. So I watch the Sun for storms all day.
drone.lore_moon: From the Moon, Earth hardly moves across the sky. Near the south pole, it hangs low.
drone.lore2_moon: Footprints on the Moon can last for millions of years. There is no wind to blow them away.
drone.drillIntro: Drill time! A block slides along the top. Drop it right on the stack to build the shelter.
drone.win: Beep! Strong shelter! On the mission, use the Build up the shelter job. Then everyone gets fewer space rays.
drone.drillIntro_moon: Drill time! The scoop slides by itself. Pour dirt on every part!

mission.storm: I watch the Sun for you. In a solar storm, astronauts in the shelter get fewer space rays. A thicker shelter helps even more.
mission.dust: Even during dust season, the Sun can send space rays. Near the end of this mission, I may beep a warning. Then the shelter matters!
mission.moon: The Moon has no thick air to block space rays. When the Sun sends a storm, get into the shelter fast.

comfort.title: Comfort
comfort.calm: Calm mode: nothing shakes, flashes or blows
comfort.saved: These settings stay on this device.

wipe.hint: Rub the dust off with your finger or mouse. Keys: ← → pick a panel, Space rubs.

build.hint: Drag one part onto the base. Or pick a part, then its spot.
build.holding: You are holding: {{part}}. Now choose its spot.
build.missed: Drop the part on a spot of the base.
build.keep: Keep the parts and save the power

radio.hint: Hold Send to power the dish. Then watch your question fly to Earth.
radio.ready: Earth is {{n}} light-minutes away right now.
radio.tooShort: Hold a little longer. The dish needs power.
radio.flying: Your question is flying to Earth
radio.arrived: Earth got your question after {{n}} minutes. The answer comes back tonight.
radio.skip: Stay quiet and save the power

heater.hint: Tonight is very cold. Turn the heater dial, then say good night.
heater.off: Off: the crew huddles together and eats more.
heater.on: On: the heater keeps everyone warm.

engineering.title: Engineering bay
engineering.lead: Real NASA numbers, drawn as blocks. A longer bar means a bigger number. For cold, longer means colder.

power.title: Dust steals power
power.caption: A dust storm darkened the sky and cut InSight's power by about a third.

cold.title: Freezing nights
cold.caption: One night at Gale Crater dropped to −71 °C. Ice melts at 0 °C.

rays.title: Space rays
rays.day: A quiet day at Gale Crater
rays.caption: In May 2024, one solar storm gave Curiosity about as many space rays as 40 quiet days. A rough comparison.

step.start: Press Start mission to fly to your Mars base.
step.goal: Your goal: earn these 3 stars by the end of the mission.
step.drive: Drive the rover to a rock, then bring it home.
step.endSol: Every astronaut has a job. Now press End sol.
step.report: See what your plan did, then go on.
